newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore libel trial starts under spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Singapore libel trial starts under spotlight.

text.p: Singapore's leaders went to court again on Monday to accuse an opposition figure of defamation in a case being monitored by international human rights bodies.
"Battle is to be joined," Workers' Party leader Joshua Jeyaretnam, target of 11 suits, told reporters after long private discussions in the judge's chambers.

Court officials said possible settlements had been discussed to the cases brought against Jeyaretnam by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, his predecessor Lee Kuan Yew and nine other top members of the ruling People's Action Party (PAP). They declined to elaborate.
The case, the latest legal clash of many between Jeyaretnam and the PAP, drew a huge crowd and left many outside the jammed courtroom.
It also drew international attention.

"Amnesty International is concerned at reports that the Government of Singapore has used civil defamation suits against political opponents in a manner that violates their right to freely hold and peacefully express their convictions," the London-based organisation said in a statement.
The PAP leadership vehemently denies using the courts to silence the opposition. It was a question, Goh said earlier this year, of challenging allegations that would undermine his ability to govern.

Their case is the second this year against a member of the Workers' Party and both sides have brought in top London libel for a case also being monitored by the Geneva-based International Commission of Jurists (ICJ).

As in the first trial, the allegations stem from December's general election campaign when the PAP, which romped to victory in 81 of parliament's 83 seats, turned all its weapons on Workers' Party candidate Tang Liang Hong.
They accused Tang of being "an anti-Christian, Chinese chauvinist" who endangered racial harmony in predominantly ethnic Chinese Singapore, which has substantial minorities of Malays and Tamils.
Tang filed complaints to the police charging Goh and his colleagues with lying. They sued him, and Tang fled Singapore saying his life had been threatened.

He did not return to defend himself in the libel actions and the cases were awarded to the PAP leaders. They won a record S$8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in damages and then sued Jeyaretnam, accusing him of endorsing Tang's charge of lying while speaking to a campaign rally.
"Mr Tang Liang Hong has just placed before me two reports he has made to police against, you know, Mr Goh Chok Tong and his people," Jeyaretnam told a campaign rally.
Goh's legal team said in its opening statement that the comment amounted to an endorsement of Tang's charges.

"The reaction of the crowd to the mention of the police report makes it clear that they were in no doubt as to what the defendant, himself an experienced lawyer and known to be such, was alleging," it said.
Jeyaretnam, who brought in libel expert George Carman to defend him, denied any intent to defame. "I can't see those words meaning what they say," he told reporters.
Jeyaretnam has paid damages of more than S$780,000 (US$553,000) over the years to former prime minister Lee, his main PAP courtroom opponent.
In the most famous of Jeyaretnam's legal battles, he and a co-defendant were jailed for a month and fined S$5,000 in 1986 for making false statement over Workers' Party accounts.

He appealed to London's Privy Council, the highest court for many Commonwealth nations. It said Jeyaretnam and his co-defendant had been "publicly disgraced for offences of which they were not guilty", although the finding was only advisory.
Singapore later abolished appeals to the Privy Council.
